rationale: Clinical delineation of FBXO11-related intellectual developmental disorder with dysmorphic facies and behavioral abnormalities reveals an exceptionally broad, non-specific neurodevelopmental spectrum (intellectual disability, ADHD/autistic/aggressive behavior, hypotonia, thin upper lip). While classical hallmarks of Coffin-Siris syndrome (such as hypoplastic fifth fingernails/toenails and hypertrichosis) and Koolen-de Vries syndrome (pear-shaped nose, friendly personality) are typically considered absent in typical FBXO11 presentations, multiple large clinical series demonstrate that FBXO11 lacks a sufficiently recognizable syndromic gestalt on phenotype alone, necessitating reverse phenotyping from molecular sequencing. Furthermore, the provided sources show overlap and frequent differential consideration with Coffin-Siris syndrome and BAFopathies, while providing no systematic evidence that clinical criteria alone reliably distinguish FBXO11 from Koolen-de Vries syndrome.

evidence.text: Detailed clinical evaluation of 24 individuals with de novo FBXO11 variants revealed mild to severe intellectual disability, variable behavioral disturbances (ADHD, ASD, anxiety, aggression), hypotonia, and subtle facial traits (thin upper lip, broad space between peaks of the upper lip), highlighting that individuals did not initially appear to possess a clear recognizable gestalt and required reverse phenotyping.

source.title: De novo variants in FBXO11 cause a syndromic form of ... - PMC
source.quote: Determining pathogenicity of genomic variation identified by next-generation sequencing techniques can be supported by recurrent disruptive variants in the same gene in phenotypically similar individuals. However, interpretation of novel variants in a specific gene in individuals with mild-moderate intellectual disability (ID) without recognizable syndromic features can be challenging and reverse phenotyping is often required. We describe 24 individuals with a de novo disease-causing variant in, or partial deletion of, the F-box only protein 11 gene (FBXO11, also known as VIT1 and PRMT9).

evidence.text: In a cohort assembling 23 additional individuals with de novo FBXO11 variants, the clinical phenotype remained highly variable with intellectual disability, behavioral anomalies, and facial dysmorphisms without a single pathognomonic gestalt, noting comparison and overlap with syndromes such as Coffin-Siris syndrome (ARID1B).

evidence.text: Targeted next-generation sequencing of 92 patients with syndromic intellectual disability demonstrated significant clinical and genetic heterogeneity, diagnosing de novo candidate variants in FBXO11 alongside distinct diagnoses of Coffin-Siris syndrome, demonstrating that unbiased genomic screening is necessary rather than reliance on strict phenotypic exclusion.

source.title: High diagnostic yield of syndromic intellectual disability by targeted next-generation sequencing
source.quote: Additionally, seven de novo probably pathogenic mutations were found in the candidate genes AGO1, JARID2, SIN3B, FBXO11, MAP3K7, HDAC2 and SMARCC2. Altogether, this means a diagnostic yield of 39% of the cases (95% CI 30% to 49%).

conflicts: Published FBXO11 cohorts (Jansen et al. 2019, Gregor et al. 2022) emphasize that individuals present with subtle, non-specific dysmorphism without a distinct pathognomonic facial gestalt, making phenotypic-only discrimination from overlapping syndromes unreliable without genomic sequencing.

The available literature in the sources block provides no direct validation that Koolen-de Vries syndrome (KANSL1) can be reliably differentiated from FBXO11 purely based on the absence of pear-shaped nose or hyper-affability.

new_directions.question_text: Can computational deep-phenotyping algorithms (e.g., PhenoScore or GestaltMatcher) reliably discriminate FBXO11-associated facial features from Coffin-Siris syndrome and Koolen-de Vries syndrome cohorts?
new_directions.rationale: Because human clinical inspection often fails to identify distinct syndromic features in FBXO11, automated quantitative phenomic and facial analysis tools could determine whether subtle sub-visual facial dysmorphism patterns can distinguish them.

new_directions.question_text: What is the systematic prevalence of distal digital and nail hypoplasia in an aggregated international cohort of FBXO11 patients?
new_directions.rationale: Clarifying the exact penetrance of nail/phalanx anomalies across all documented FBXO11 patients will definitively test whether nail hypoplasia serves as an absolute negative discriminator against Coffin-Siris syndrome.
